claim: Cortical areas form a hierarchy of intrinsic timescales.
source: Cortical areas seem to form a hierarchy of intrinsic timescales, but the relevance of this organization for cognitive behavior remains unknown.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: The relevance of the cortical timescale hierarchy for cognitive behavior remains unknown.
source: Cortical areas seem to form a hierarchy of intrinsic timescales, but the relevance of this organization for cognitive behavior remains unknown.
evidence: Statement about the state of knowledge in the field

claim: Decisions requiring gradual accrual of sensory evidence over time recruit widespread areas across the cortical hierarchy.
source: In particular, decisions requiring the gradual accrual of sensory evidence over time recruit widespread areas across this hierarchy.
evidence: Statement based on established findings in the field

claim: The recruitment of widespread cortical areas during evidence accumulation is related to the intrinsic integration timescales of these areas.
source: Here, we tested the hypothesis that this recruitment is related to the intrinsic integration timescales of these widespread areas.
evidence: This is the main hypothesis tested in the study

claim: Mice were trained to accumulate evidence over seconds while navigating in virtual reality.
source: We trained mice to accumulate evidence over seconds while navigating in virtual reality and optogenetically silenced the activity of many cortical areas during different brief trial epochs.
evidence: Description of experimental methods performed

claim: Inactivation of all tested cortical areas affected the evidence-accumulation computation.
source: We found that the inactivation of all tested areas affected the evidence-accumulation computation.
evidence: Main finding from the optogenetic inactivation experiments

claim: Frontal inactivations led to stronger deficits on long timescales than posterior cortical inactivations.
source: Specifically, we observed distinct changes in the weighting of sensory evidence occurring during and before silencing, such that frontal inactivations led to stronger deficits on long timescales than posterior cortical ones.
evidence: Main finding comparing frontal and posterior cortical areas

claim: Inactivation of a subset of frontal areas led to moderate effects on behavioral processes beyond evidence accumulation.
source: Inactivation of a subset of frontal areas also led to moderate effects on behavioral processes beyond evidence accumulation.
evidence: Finding from the inactivation experiments

claim: Large-scale cortical Ca2+ activity during task performance displayed different temporal integration windows.
source: Moreover, large-scale cortical Ca2+ activity during task performance displayed different temporal integration windows.
evidence: Finding from widefield calcium imaging experiments

claim: The intrinsic timescale hierarchy of distributed cortical areas is an important component of evidence-accumulation mechanisms.
source: Our findings suggest that the intrinsic timescale hierarchy of distributed cortical areas is an important component of evidence-accumulation mechanisms.
evidence: Main conclusion drawn from the experimental findings

claim: The cerebral cortex of both rodents and primates is organized in a hierarchy of intrinsic integration timescales, with frontal areas integrating input over longer time windows than sensory areas.
source: The cerebral cortex of both rodents and primates appears to be organized in a hierarchy of intrinsic integration timescales, whereby frontal areas integrate input over longer time windows than sensory areas (Cavanagh et al., 2020; Chaudhuri et al., 2015; Gao et al., 2020; Hasson et al., 2008; Ito et al., 2020; Kiebel et al., 2008; Murray et al., 2014; Runyan et al., 2017; Soltani et al., 2021; Spitmaan et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior literature

claim: The role of the cortical timescale hierarchy in cognitive behavior remains unclear.
source: Although this idea has received increasing attention, the role of such timescale hierarchy in cognitive behavior remains unclear.
evidence: Statement about the state of knowledge in the field

claim: Evidence accumulation involves remembering a running tally of evidence, updating that tally when new evidence becomes available, and making a choice based on the predominant evidence.
source: This involves remembering a running tally of evidence for or against a decision, updating that tally when new evidence becomes available, and making a choice based on the predominant evidence (Bogacz et al., 2006; Brody and Hanks, 2016; Brunton et al., 2013; Carandini and Churchland, 2013; Gold and Shadlen, 2007; Morcos and Harvey, 2016; Newsome et al., 1989; Odoemene et al., 2018; Stine et al., 2020; Sun and Landy, 2016; Tsetsos et al., 2012; Waskom and Kiani, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: Neural correlates of decisions relying on evidence accumulation have been found in a number of cortical and subcortical structures in both primates and rodents.
source: Neural correlates of decisions relying on evidence accumulation have been found in a number of cortical and subcortical structures, in both primates and rodents (Brincat et al., 2018; Ding and Gold, 2010; Erlich et al., 2015; Hanks et al., 2015; Horwitz and Newsome, 1999; Kim and Shadlen, 1999; Koay et al., 2020; Krueger et al., 2017; Murphy et al., 2021; Orsolic et al., 2021; Scott et al., 2017; Shadlen and Newsome, 2001; Wilming et al., 2020; Yartsev et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: When mice must accumulate evidence over several seconds to make a navigational decision, the inactivation of widespread dorsal cortical areas leads to behavioral deficits.
source: Likewise, we have previously shown that, when mice must accumulate evidence over several seconds to make a navigational decision, the inactivation of widespread dorsal cortical areas leads to behavioral deficits, and that these areas encode multiple behavioral variables, including evidence (Pinto et al., 2019).
evidence: Reference to previous work by the authors

claim: Widespread dorsal cortical areas encode multiple behavioral variables, including evidence.
source: Likewise, we have previously shown that, when mice must accumulate evidence over several seconds to make a navigational decision, the inactivation of widespread dorsal cortical areas leads to behavioral deficits, and that these areas encode multiple behavioral variables, including evidence (Pinto et al., 2019).
evidence: Reference to previous work by the authors

claim: The aspects of decisions that lead to widespread recruitment of brain structures during evidence accumulation are not understood.
source: However, we do not understand which aspects of these decisions lead to such widespread recruitment of brain structures.
evidence: Statement about the state of knowledge in the field

claim: The inactivation of different cortical areas affects accumulation over distinct timescales, with frontal areas contributing to evidence memory over longer temporal windows than posterior areas.
source: Further, the inactivation of different areas affects accumulation over distinct timescales, such that, to an approximation, frontal areas contribute to evidence memory over longer temporal windows than posterior areas.
evidence: Main finding from the inactivation experiments

claim: Cortical activity during the accumulation task displays a gradient of intrinsic timescales, which are longer in frontal areas.
source: In agreement with this, we show that cortical activity during the accumulation task displays a gradient of intrinsic timescales, which are longer in frontal areas.
evidence: Finding from widefield calcium imaging experiments

claim: The existing cortical hierarchy of temporal integration windows is important for evidence-accumulation computations.
source: Our findings thus suggest the existing cortical hierarchy of temporal integration windows is important for evidence-accumulation computations.
evidence: Main conclusion drawn from the experimental findings

claim: Task performance was modulated by the difference in tower counts between the right and left sides.
source: Compatible with our previous reports (Koay et al., 2020; Pinto et al., 2018), task performance was modulated by the difference in tower counts between the right and left sides (Figure 1B, n=28).
evidence: Behavioral data shown in Figure 1B and referenced to prior work

claim: On average, mice weighted evidence equally from throughout the maze.
source: While individual mice showed different evidence-weighting profiles, fitting the model on aggregate data yielded a flat evidence-weighting curve (Figure 1C, n=108,940 trials), indicating that on average the mice weighted evidence equally from throughout the maze (Pinto et al., 2018).
evidence: Logistic regression analysis shown in Figure 1C and referenced to prior work

claim: Seven different cortical areas were targeted for optogenetic inactivation: V1, mV2, PPC, RSC, mM2, aM2, and M1.
source: We targeted seven different areas – primary visual cortex (V1), medial secondary visual cortex (mV2, roughly corresponding to area AM), posterior parietal cortex (PPC), retrosplenial cortex (RSC), the posteromedial portion of the premotor cortex (mM2), the anterior portion of the premotor cortex (aM2), and the primary motor cortex (M1) – as well as two combinations of these individual areas, namely posterior cortex (V1, mV2, PPC, and RSC) and frontal cortex (mM2, aM2, and M1).
evidence: Description of experimental methods

claim: Cortical silencing occurred in one of six trial epochs.
source: Cortical silencing occurred in one of six trial epochs: first, second , or third quarter of the cue region (0–50 cm, 50–100 cm, or 100–150 cm, respectively), first or second half of the cue region (0–100 cm or 100–200 cm, respectively), or delay region (200–300 cm).
evidence: Description of experimental methods

claim: A total of 54 possible area-epoch combinations were tested.
source: We tested all 54 possible area-epoch combinations (Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: Description of experimental design

claim: The inactivation of all tested cortical areas significantly affected behavioral performance, though to varying degrees.
source: Compatible with our previous whole-trial inactivation experiments (Pinto et al., 2019), we found that the inactivation of all tested cortical areas significantly affected behavioral performance, though to varying degrees (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Behavioral data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1, referenced to prior work

claim: Different effects were observed even comparing regions that were in close physical proximity.
source: Although our previous measurements indicate inactivation spreads of at least 2 mm (Pinto et al., 2019), we observed different effects even comparing regions that were in close physical proximity (e.g. V1 and mV2).
evidence: Observation from the inactivation experiments, referenced to prior work

claim: All tested areas had significant effects in at least a subset of conditions.
source: Additionally, all tested areas had significant effects in at least a subset of conditions (Figure 1—figure supplement 2, p<0.05, bootstrapping).
evidence: Statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: Inactivation resulted in minor changes in running speed in a subset of conditions, with an average overall increase of ~8%.
source: Finally, in agreement with our previous results (Pinto et al., 2019), inactivation resulted in minor changes in running speed in a subset of conditions (average overall increase of ~8%, Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Behavioral data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3, referenced to prior work

claim: The effects of optogenetic inactivation are specific to mice expressing ChR2, ruling out a non-specific light effect.
source: Importantly, we have previously shown that these effects are specific to mice expressing ChR2, ruling out a non-specific light effect (Pinto et al., 2019).
evidence: Reference to control experiments in prior work

claim: Changes in the weighting of sensory evidence occurring before laser onset primarily reflect effects on the memory of past evidence.
source: We reasoned that changes in the weighting of sensory evidence occurring before laser onset would primarily reflect effects on the memory of past evidence, while changes in evidence occurring while the laser was on would reflect disruption of processing and/or very short-term memory of the evidence.
evidence: Reasoning about the interpretation of experimental results

claim: Changes in evidence weighting during laser-on periods reflect disruption of processing and/or very short-term memory of the evidence.
source: We reasoned that changes in the weighting of sensory evidence occurring before laser onset would primarily reflect effects on the memory of past evidence, while changes in evidence occurring while the laser was on would reflect disruption of processing and/or very short-term memory of the evidence.
evidence: Reasoning about the interpretation of experimental results

claim: Changes in evidence weighting following laser offset potentially indicate effects on processes beyond accumulation per se, such as commitment to a decision.
source: Finally, changes in evidence weighting following laser offset would potentially indicate effects on processes beyond accumulation per se, such as commitment to a decision.
evidence: Reasoning about the interpretation of experimental results

claim: A perturbation that caused a premature commitment to a decision would lead to towers that appeared subsequent to the perturbation having no weight on the animal's choice.
source: For example, a perturbation that caused a premature commitment to a decision would lead to towers that appeared subsequent to the perturbation having no weight on the animal's choice.
evidence: Reasoning about the interpretation of experimental results

claim: Mixed-effects logistic regression models accurately predicted ~70% of behavioral choices in trials not used to fit the data.
source: Overall, these models accurately predicted ~70% of behavioral choices in trials not used to fit the data (Figure 2B).
evidence: Model performance shown in Figure 2B

claim: PPC inactivation only led to significant decreases in the use of sensory evidence occurring during inactivation or immediately preceding it.
source: For instance, PPC inactivation only led to significant decreases in the use of sensory evidence occurring during inactivation or immediately preceding it (Figure 2A, p<0.001, t-test), indicating a role in processing and memory of very recent sensory evidence (≤0.5 s).
evidence: Statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 2A

claim: PPC has a role in processing and memory of very recent sensory evidence (≤0.5 s).
source: For instance, PPC inactivation only led to significant decreases in the use of sensory evidence occurring during inactivation or immediately preceding it (Figure 2A, p<0.001, t-test), indicating a role in processing and memory of very recent sensory evidence (≤0.5 s).
evidence: Inference from the inactivation data shown in Figure 2A

claim: Inactivation of all posterior areas led to deficits in the use of sensory evidence during the inactivation period, except for RSC.
source: Similarly, we observed deficits in the use of sensory evidence during the inactivation period for all posterior areas (p<0.001, t-test), except for RSC (p>0.05).
evidence: Statistical analysis of inactivation data

claim: Inactivation of mV2 only affected evidence memory on intermediate timescales (0.5–1.0 s).
source: Inactivation of mV2 only affected evidence memory on intermediate timescales (0.5–1.0 s, p<0.001, t-test).
evidence: Statistical analysis of inactivation data

claim: V1 and RSC inactivation led to non-monotonic changes in evidence memory, affecting recent (≤0.5 s) and long-past evidence (1.0–1.5 s), but not evidence occurring in between (0.5–1.0 s).
source: Conversely, V1 and RSC inactivation led to non-monotonic changes in evidence memory, affecting recent (≤0.5 s, p<0.001) and long-past evidence (1.0–1.5 s, p<0.001), but not evidence occurring in between (0.5–1.0 s, p>0.05).
evidence: Statistical analysis of inactivation data

claim: For all posterior cortical areas, significant changes in the evidence-weighting curves happened exclusively for evidence concomitant to or preceding laser onset.
source: Lastly, for all posterior cortical areas, significant changes in the evidence-weighting curves happened exclusively for evidence concomitant to or preceding laser onset, indicating that the manipulations primarily affected the processing and/or memory of the evidence, i.e., the accumulation process itself.
evidence: Analysis of inactivation data

claim: Inactivation of posterior cortical areas primarily affected the processing and/or memory of the evidence, i.e., the accumulation process itself.
source: Lastly, for all posterior cortical areas, significant changes in the evidence-weighting curves happened exclusively for evidence concomitant to or preceding laser onset, indicating that the manipulations primarily affected the processing and/or memory of the evidence, i.e., the accumulation process itself.
evidence: Inference from the inactivation data

claim: Inactivation of all three frontal areas (M1, mM2, aM2) led to profound deficits in the use of long-past evidence (1.0–1.5 s).
source: Notably, inactivation of all three frontal areas (M1, mM2, aM2) led to profound deficits in the use of long-past evidence (1.0–1.5 s, p<0.001, t-test), but only aM2 inactivation led to changes in the use of evidence occurring while the laser was on (p<0.001).
evidence: Statistical analysis of inactivation data

claim: Only aM2 inactivation led to changes in the use of evidence occurring while the laser was on.
source: Notably, inactivation of all three frontal areas (M1, mM2, aM2) led to profound deficits in the use of long-past evidence (1.0–1.5 s, p<0.001, t-test), but only aM2 inactivation led to changes in the use of evidence occurring while the laser was on (p<0.001).
evidence: Statistical analysis of inactivation data

claim: Inactivation of mM2 and M1 led to significant changes in the use of sensory evidence occurring after laser offset.
source: Interestingly, inactivation of mM2 and M1 also led to significant changes in the use of sensory evidence occurring after laser offset (p<0.001), although to a lesser extent than pre-laser evidence (Figure 2A).
evidence: Statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 2A

claim: Frontal areas may have a role in post-stimulus categorization or commitment to a decision, in addition to evidence accumulation.
source: This could indicate that, in addition to evidence accumulation, these frontal areas also have a role in other decision processes, such as post-stimulus categorization (Hanks et al., 2015) or commitment to a decision.
evidence: Inference from the inactivation data, with citation to prior work

claim: Silencing frontal regions could result in a premature decision.
source: In this case, silencing these regions could result in a premature decision.
evidence: Speculation about the interpretation of experimental results

claim: Frontal and posterior areas differed significantly in terms of the magnitude and time course of evidence-weighting deficits induced by their inactivation.
source: Indeed, frontal and posterior areas differed significantly in terms of the magnitude and time course of evidence-weighting deficits induced by their inactivation (Figure 2C, two-way repeated measure ANOVA with factors time bin and area group; F[time]5,15 = 3.09, p[time]=0.047, F[area]1,3 = 33.93, p[area]=0.010, F[interaction]5,15 = 3.60, p[interaction]=0.025).
evidence: Statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 2C

claim: Compared to posterior areas, frontal inactivation resulted in a significantly larger decrease in the use of sensory evidence occurring long before laser onset (1.0–1.5 s).
source: In particular, compared to posterior areas, frontal inactivation resulted in a significantly larger decrease in the use of sensory evidence occurring long before laser onset (1.0–1.5 s, p=0.006, z-test).
evidence: Statistical analysis of inactivation data

claim: Frontal inactivation led to decreases in the use of sensory evidence occurring after inactivation.
source: Moreover, it led to decreases in the use of sensory evidence occurring after inactivation (p<0.001, z-test).
evidence: Statistical analysis of inactivation data

claim: Both posterior and frontal simultaneous inactivations significantly deviated from the even-combination prediction.
source: Both posterior and frontal significantly deviated from the even-combination prediction (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, p<0.05, z-test).
evidence: Statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: Signals from different dorsal cortical areas may be combined with different weights toward a final decision.
source: This could suggest that signals from the different dorsal cortical areas are combined with different weights toward a final decision.
evidence: Inference from the simultaneous inactivation data

claim: Different regions of the dorsal cortex contribute to distinct aspects of evidence-accumulation-based decisions.
source: Our inactivation results thus suggest that different regions of the dorsal cortex contribute to distinct aspects of evidence-accumulation-based decisions.
evidence: Summary of inactivation findings

claim: All tested cortical areas have a role in evidence accumulation, but they do so on distinct timescales.
source: In particular, while all areas we tested appear to have a role in evidence accumulation, they do so on distinct timescales.
evidence: Summary of inactivation findings

claim: Cortical timescale hierarchies are thought to arise in part from intrinsic cellular and circuit properties such as channel and receptor expression, amount of recurrent connectivity, and relative proportions of inhibitory interneuron subtypes.
source: While these are thought to arise in part from intrinsic cellular and circuit properties such as channel and receptor expression, amount of recurrent connectivity, and relative proportions of inhibitory interneuron subtypes (Chaudhuri et al., 2015; Duarte et al., 2017; Fulcher et al., 2019; Gao et al., 2020; Wang, 2020), they appear to be modulated by task demands (Gao et al., 2020; Ito et al., 2020; Zeraati et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: Cortical timescale hierarchies appear to be modulated by task demands.
source: While these are thought to arise in part from intrinsic cellular and circuit properties such as channel and receptor expression, amount of recurrent connectivity, and relative proportions of inhibitory interneuron subtypes (Chaudhuri et al., 2015; Duarte et al., 2017; Fulcher et al., 2019; Gao et al., 2020; Wang, 2020), they appear to be modulated by task demands (Gao et al., 2020; Ito et al., 2020; Zeraati et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: Adding coupling and auto-regressive predictors to the encoding model resulted in a large and significant increase in cross-validated model accuracy.
source: Adding these new sets of predictors resulted in a large and significant increase in cross-validated model accuracy, as measured by the linear correlation coefficient between the model predictions and a test dataset not used to fit the model (Figure 4B and C; ~0.95 vs. ~0.3, Fmodel (6,2,12) = 1994.85, p=6.2 × 10–13, two-way ANOVA with repeated measures).
evidence: Statistical analysis of model performance shown in Figure 4B and C

claim: The rate of decay of auto-regressive coefficients over lags slowed systematically from visual to premotor areas, with intermediate values for M1, PPC, and RSC.
source: We observed that across animals the rate of decay of these coefficients over lags slowed systematically from visual to premotor areas, with intermediate values for M1, PPC, and RSC (Figure 4D).
evidence: Analysis of encoding model coefficients shown in Figure 4D

claim: Decay time constants (τ) differed significantly across cortical areas, being larger for frontal than posterior areas.
source: Compatible with our observations, τ differed significantly across cortical areas (F6,30 = 4.49, p=0.006, one-way ANOVA with repeated measures), being larger for frontal than posterior areas.
evidence: Statistical analysis of decay time constants

claim: During the evidence-accumulation task, cortical regions display increasing intrinsic timescales going from visual to frontal areas.
source: Thus, during the evidence-accumulation task, cortical regions display increasing intrinsic timescales going from visual to frontal areas.
evidence: Summary of encoding model findings

claim: The finding that cortical regions display increasing intrinsic timescales from visual to frontal areas is consistent with previous reports for spontaneous activity and other behavioral tasks.
source: This is consistent with previous reports for spontaneous activity and other behavioral tasks (Chaudhuri et al., 2015; Hasson et al., 2008; Murray et al., 2014; Runyan et al., 2017) and is compatible with our inactivation findings (Figures 2 and 3).
evidence: Comparison to prior literature and to the inactivation findings

claim: Distributed cortical areas contribute to sensory-evidence accrual on different timescales.
source: Taken together, our results suggest that distributed cortical areas contribute to sensory-evidence accrual on different timescales.
evidence: Summary of main findings

claim: On average, the inactivation of frontal cortical areas resulted in larger decreases in the use of evidence occurring further in the past from laser onset compared to posterior regions.
source: Specifically, brief sub-trial inactivations during performance of a decision-making task requiring seconds-long evidence accumulation resulted in distinct deficits in the weighting of sensory evidence from different points in the stimulus stream. This was such that, on average, the inactivation of frontal cortical areas resulted in larger decreases in the use of evidence occurring further in the past from laser onset compared to posterior regions (Figures 2 and 3).
evidence: Summary of inactivation findings shown in Figures 2 and 3

claim: Activity timescales vary systematically across the cortex in a way that mirrors the inactivation results.
source: Compatible with this, using an encoding model of large-scale cortical dynamics, we found that activity timescales vary systematically across the cortex in a way that mirrors the inactivation results (Figure 4).
evidence: Summary of encoding model findings shown in Figure 4

claim: The contributions of different cortical areas to decision-making computations are arranged in a temporal hierarchy.
source: Our results add to a growing body of literature that has revealed that the cortex of rodents and primates appears to be organized in a hierarchy of temporal processing windows across regions (Chaudhuri et al., 2015; Gao et al., 2020; Hasson et al., 2008; Ito et al., 2020; Murray et al., 2014; Runyan et al., 2017; Spitmaan et al., 2020). Specifically, they suggest that the contributions of different cortical areas to decision-making computations are similarly arranged in a temporal hierarchy.
evidence: Interpretation of findings in the context of prior literature

claim: The inactivation findings did not exactly match the same area ordering of integration windows from the widefield imaging neural data.
source: A caveat here is that our inactivation findings did not exactly match the same area ordering of integration windows from the widefield imaging neural data, nor were all the inactivation effects monotonic.
evidence: Observation about the relationship between inactivation and imaging findings

claim: Not all the inactivation effects were monotonic.
source: A caveat here is that our inactivation findings did not exactly match the same area ordering of integration windows from the widefield imaging neural data, nor were all the inactivation effects monotonic.
evidence: Observation about the inactivation findings

claim: The laser powers used result in large inactivation spreads, potentially encompassing neighboring regions.
source: This could be in part due to technical limitations of the experiments. First, the laser powers we used result in large inactivation spreads, potentially encompassing neighboring regions.
evidence: Discussion of technical limitations

claim: Local inactivation could result in changes in the activity of interconnected regions.
source: Moreover, local inactivation could result in changes in the activity of interconnected regions (Young et al., 2000), a possibility that should be evaluated in future studies using simultaneous inactivation and large-scale recordings across the dorsal cortex.
evidence: Discussion of technical limitations with citation to prior work

claim: Diverse timescales exist at the level of individual neurons within each cortical region.
source: At face value, however, the findings could be a reflection of the fact that diverse timescales exist at the level of individual neurons within each region (Bernacchia et al., 2011; Cavanagh et al., 2020; Scott et al., 2017; Spitmaan et al., 2020; Wasmuht et al., 2018).
evidence: Interpretation of findings with citations to prior literature

claim: Inactivating an area with multimodal distributions of intrinsic timescales across its neurons could conceivably result in non-monotonic effects of inactivation.
source: For example, inactivating an area with multimodal distributions of intrinsic timescales across its neurons could conceivably result in non-monotonic effects of inactivation.
evidence: Speculation about the interpretation of experimental results

claim: Accrual timescale hierarchies are a significant factor contributing to the widespread recruitment of cortical dynamics during evidence-based decisions.
source: In any case, our results point to accrual timescale hierarchies being a significant factor contributing to the widespread recruitment of cortical dynamics during evidence-based decisions, as areas get potentially progressively recruited with increasing integration timescale demands.
evidence: Interpretation of findings

claim: Areas get potentially progressively recruited with increasing integration timescale demands.
source: In any case, our results point to accrual timescale hierarchies being a significant factor contributing to the widespread recruitment of cortical dynamics during evidence-based decisions, as areas get potentially progressively recruited with increasing integration timescale demands.
evidence: Interpretation of findings

claim: The logic of widespread recruitment of cortical regions in complex, time-extended decisions may in part rely on intrinsic temporal integration properties of local cortical circuits, rather than specific evidence-accumulation mechanisms.
source: Our findings also suggest the possibility that the logic of widespread recruitment of cortical regions in complex, time-extended decisions may in part rely on intrinsic temporal integration properties of local cortical circuits, rather than specific evidence-accumulation mechanisms.
evidence: Interpretation of findings

claim: Simple perceptual decisions may primarily engage only the relevant sensory areas because they can be made on the fast intrinsic timescales displayed by these regions.
source: For instance, it is possible that simple perceptual decisions primarily engage only the relevant sensory areas because they can be made on the fast intrinsic timescales displayed by these regions (Zatka-Haas et al., 2021).
evidence: Speculation with citation to prior work

claim: Discrepancies in the literature regarding the effects of perturbing different cortical areas during evidence accumulation may stem in part from differences in the timescales of the various tasks.
source: Along the same lines, it is conceivable that discrepancies in the literature regarding the effects of perturbing different cortical areas during evidence accumulation stem in part from differences in the timescales of the various tasks (Erlich et al., 2015; Fetsch et al., 2018; Hanks et al., 2015; Katz et al., 2016; Pinto et al., 2019).
evidence: Speculation with citations to prior work

claim: An important remaining question is whether evidence from the different time windows is accumulated in parallel or as a feedforward computation going from areas with short to those with long integration time constants.
source: An important remaining question is whether evidence from the different time windows is accumulated in parallel or as a feedforward computation going from areas with short to those with long integration time constants.
evidence: Statement about open questions

claim: The parallel scheme would be compatible with recent psychophysical findings in humans reporting confidence of their evidence-based decisions.
source: The parallel scheme would be compatible with recent psychophysical findings in humans reporting confidence of their evidence-based decisions (Ganupuru et al., 2019).
evidence: Speculation with citation to prior work

claim: A feedforward transformation would be in agreement with human fMRI findings during language processing.
source: Conversely, a feedforward transformation would be in agreement with human fMRI findings during language processing (Yeshurun et al., 2017) and with a previously published model whereby successive (feedforward) convolution operations lead to progressively longer-lasting responses to sensory evidence (Scott et al., 2017).
evidence: Speculation with citations to prior work

claim: The oculomotor integrator of both fish and monkeys appears to be organized as largely feedforward chains of integration leading to systematically increasing time constants.
source: Interestingly, the oculomotor integrator of both fish and monkeys appears to be organized as largely feedforward chains of integration leading to systematically increasing time constants (Joshua and Lisberger, 2015; Miri et al., 2011), perhaps suggesting that this architecture is universal to neural integrators.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: The feedforward chain architecture may be universal to neural integrators.
source: Interestingly, the oculomotor integrator of both fish and monkeys appears to be organized as largely feedforward chains of integration leading to systematically increasing time constants (Joshua and Lisberger, 2015; Miri et al., 2011), perhaps suggesting that this architecture is universal to neural integrators.
evidence: Speculation based on prior literature

claim: It is unclear how and where evidence information from different timescales is combined to yield a final decision.
source: Finally, it is also unclear how and where evidence information from different timescales is combined to yield a final decision.
evidence: Statement about open questions

claim: Dorsal cortical activity is unevenly weighted, potentially by downstream structures.
source: Our simultaneous inactivation experiments (Figure 3) suggest that dorsal cortical activity is unevenly weighted, potentially by downstream structures.
evidence: Inference from the simultaneous inactivation data shown in Figure 3

claim: Candidate regions for combining evidence information include the medial prefrontal cortex or subcortical structures such as the striatum and the cerebellum.
source: Candidate regions include the medial prefrontal cortex or subcortical structures such as the striatum and the cerebellum, which have been shown to be causally involved in evidence accumulation (Bolkan et al., 2022; Deverett et al., 2019; Yartsev et al., 2018).
evidence: Speculation with citations to prior work

claim: Other subcortical candidates for combining evidence information are midbrain regions shown to have a high incidence of choice signals in a contrast discrimination task.
source: Other subcortical candidates are midbrain regions shown to have a high incidence of choice signals in a contrast discrimination task (Steinmetz et al., 2019).
evidence: Speculation with citation to prior work

claim: The timescale of decision processes is an important feature governing their underlying neural mechanisms.
source: Our findings highlight the fact that, much like in memory systems (Jeneson and Squire, 2012), the timescale of decision processes is an important feature governing their underlying neural mechanisms, a notion which should be incorporated into both experimental and theoretical accounts of decision making.
evidence: Interpretation of findings with citation to prior work

claim: VGAT-ChR2-EYFP mice aged 2–16 months were used for the inactivation experiments.
source: We used both male and female VGAT-ChR2-EYFP mice aged 2–16 months (B6.Cg-Tg[Slc32a1-COP4*H134R/EYFP]8Gfng/J, Jackson Laboratories, stock # 014548, n=28).
evidence: Description of experimental subjects

claim: Part of the inactivation data from some animals was collected in the context of previous work, but the analyses reported here are completely novel.
source: Part of the inactivation data from some of these animals was collected in the context of previous work (Pinto et al., 2019), but the analyses reported here are completely novel.
evidence: Statement about data provenance

claim: The widefield Ca2+ imaging analysis is from data collected in the context of a previous study, although the analysis is novel.
source: The analysis reported in Figure 4 (widefield Ca2+ imaging) is from data collected in the context of a previous study (Pinto et al., 2019), although the analysis is novel.
evidence: Statement about data provenance

claim: The widefield imaging data was from six male and female mice from triple transgenic crosses expressing GCaMP6f under the CaMKIIα promoter.
source: The data was from six male and female mice from triple transgenic crosses expressing GCaMP6f under the CaMKIIα promoter from the following two lines: Ai93-D; CaMKIIα-tTA [IgS6tm93.1(tetO-GCaMP6f)Hze Tg[Camk2a-tTA]1Mmay/J, Jackson Laboratories, stock # 024108] and Emx1-IRES-Cre [B6.129S2-Emx1tm1(cre)Krj/J, Jackson Laboratories, stock # 005628].
evidence: Description of experimental subjects

claim: Mice navigated a 3-m long virtual T-maze during the accumulating towers task.
source: The mice navigated a 3-m long virtual T-maze and during the first 2 m (~4 s) they encountered salient objects, or towers, along the walls on either side, and after a delay of 1 m (~2 s) turned into the arm corresponding to the highest perceived tower count.
evidence: Description of behavioral task

claim: Towers were visible for 200 ms and appeared at different positions in each trial.
source: The towers were visible for 200 ms and appeared at different positions in each trial, obeying spatial Poisson processes of different underlying rates on the rewarded and non-rewarded sides.
evidence: Description of behavioral task

claim: The task design decorrelated the position of individual towers from the animals' position in the maze across trials.
source: Crucially, beyond allowing us to probe sensitivity to sensory evidence, the task design decorrelated the position of individual towers from the animals' position in the maze across trials.
evidence: Description of behavioral task design

claim: A 473 nm laser beam was used for optogenetic inactivation.
source: Briefly, a 473 nm laser beam (OBIS, Coherent, Santa Clara, CA) was directed to 2D galvanometers using a 125-µm single-mode optic fiber optic (Thorlabs, Newton, NJ) and reached the cortical surface after passing through an f-theta scanning lens (LINOS, Waltham, MA).
evidence: Description of experimental methods

claim: A 40 Hz square wave with an 80% duty cycle and a power of 6 mW measured at the level of the skull was used for optogenetic inactivation.
source: We used a 40 Hz square wave with an 80% duty cycle and a power of 6 mW measured at the level of the skull.
evidence: Description of experimental methods

claim: The laser power of 6 mW corresponds to an inactivation spread of ~2 mm.
source: This corresponds to an inactivation spread of ~2 mm (Pinto et al., 2019).
evidence: Reference to prior work

claim: The effects of whole-trial inactivations at much lower powers are consistent with those obtained at 6 mW.
source: While this may introduce confounds regarding ascribing exact functions to specific cortical areas, we have previously shown that the effects of whole-trial inactivations at much lower powers (corresponding to smaller spatial spreads) are consistent with those obtained at 6 mW.
evidence: Reference to prior work

claim: The last 100 ms of the laser pulse consisted of a linear ramp-down of power to minimize post-inactivation rebounds.
source: To minimize post-inactivation rebounds, the last 100 ms of the laser pulse consisted of a linear ramp-down of power (Guo et al., 2014; Pinto et al., 2019).
evidence: Description of experimental methods with citations to prior work

claim: A total of 929 optogenetic inactivation sessions from 28 mice were analyzed, corresponding to 108,940 control trials and 29,825 inactivation trials.
source: These selection criteria yielded a total of 929 optogenetic inactivation sessions from 28 mice (average ~33 /mouse), corresponding to 108,940 control (laser off) trials, and 29,825 inactivation trials (average ~552/condition, see Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: Description of data analyzed

claim: Twenty-five sessions from six mice were selected for widefield imaging data analysis.
source: Twenty-five sessions from six mice were selected for widefield imaging data analysis.
evidence: Description of data analyzed

claim: A mixed-effects logistic regression model was used to quantify how manipulations impacted the weighting of sensory evidence in time relative to inactivation onset and offset.
source: To directly quantify how our manipulations impacted the weighting of sensory evidence in time relative to inactivation onset and offset, while accounting for variability introduced by different mice and epochs in the trial, we fitted a mixed-effects logistic regression model to the mice's choices using the Pymer4 package for Python (Jolly, 2018):
evidence: Description of analysis methods

claim: All models were fitted using 10-fold cross-validation.
source: All models were fitted using 10-fold cross-validation.
evidence: Description of analysis methods

claim: Error estimates and statistics for general performance, running speed, and logistic regression weights in space were generated by bootstrapping 10,000 times.
source: Error estimates and statistics for general performance, running speed, and logistic regression weights in space were generated by bootstrapping this procedure 10,000 times, where in each iteration we sampled trials with replacement.
evidence: Description of statistical methods

claim: False discovery rate correction was applied for multiple comparisons.
source: We corrected for multiple comparisons using a previously described method for false discovery rate correction (Benjamini and Hochberg, 1995; Guo et al., 2014; Pinto et al., 2019).
evidence: Description of statistical methods with citations to prior work

claim: An aggregate power of n=250 trials was obtained from the bootstrapping-based power analysis.
source: We obtained an aggregate power of n=250.
evidence: Result from power analysis

claim: Ca2+ activity averaged over each anatomically defined ROI was fitted with a linear model.
source: We fitted Ca2+ activity averaged over each anatomically defined ROI with a linear model (Pinto et al., 2019; Pinto and Dan, 2015; Scott et al., 2017).
evidence: Description of analysis methods with citations to prior work

claim: The encoding model included task-event predictors, coupling terms, and auto-regressive terms.
source: In addition to the previously used task-event predictors (Pinto et al., 2019), we added coupling terms, i.e., the zero-lag activity of the other simultaneously imaged ROIs (Pillow et al., 2008; Runyan et al., 2017), as well as auto-regressive terms to capture activity auto-correlations that were independent of task events (Spitmaan et al., 2020).
evidence: Description of analysis methods with citations to prior work

claim: Ridge regression was performed by adding a term to penalize the L2 norm of the coefficients.
source: Finally, we added a term to penalize the L2 norm of the coefficients, i.e., we performed ridge regression.
evidence: Description of analysis methods

claim: The significance of the differences in the time constants across regions was assessed by performing a one-way ANOVA with repeated measures.
source: The significance of the differences in the time constants across regions was assessed by performing a one-way ANOVA with repeated measures, with cortical regions as the factor.
evidence: Description of statistical methods
